title: Recovery Strategies After Physical Exercise
summary:
Recovery is an essential part of adapting to exercise, and in pregnancy it matters even more because of metabolic, hormonal, biomechanical and emotional changes. Higher plasma volume and cardiac output, elevated resting heart rate, relaxin-related ligament laxity, and higher body temperature all call for more gradual, individualized recovery. The chapter treats recovery as an active phase of training, not a passive period.

It describes active, passive, nutritional, psychological and physiotherapeutic strategies, then adapts them to aerobic, strength, core/pelvic floor and balance work and to sedentary, active and athlete profiles. It closes with sleep advice and notes that good recovery improves adherence, mood, sleep and preparation for labor.
points: Allow 24-48 h of active recovery between moderate-intensity sessions.
Monitor for excessive fatigue: RPE >15, dyspnea, dizziness or contractions.
Active recovery includes slow walking for 5-10 minutes after training, diaphragmatic breathing, light joint mobilization and dynamic stretching.
Passive recovery includes resting in the left lateral decubitus position and restorative sleep of 7-9 hours.
Drink 250-300 ml of water or an isotonic beverage immediately after exercise.
Eat a carbohydrate and protein snack (1:3 ratio) within 30 minutes, for example yogurt with oats, fruit and nuts.
Fatigue is greater in the first and third trimesters, so reduce session intensity and duration then.
Psychological tools include 4x4x4 abdominal breathing (inhale 4 s, hold 4 s, exhale 4 s), a 10-minute body scan and restorative prenatal yoga.
Pregnant athletes recover cardiovascularly well but risk more neuromuscular fatigue if they do not adapt training volume.
takeaways: Finish every session with 5-10 min of slow walking and stretching.
Drink 250-300 ml of fluid right after exercise and eat a snack within 30 minutes.
Sleep preferably on your left side, keep a regular schedule, and avoid heavy or sugary meals before bed.
Use breathing or a short body scan after sessions to lower stress.
After strength work, use passive stretches or a soft foam roller with controlled breathing.
Keep rest active: gentle movement, walking and mindful breathing rather than inactivity.
cautions: Watch for RPE >15, dyspnea, dizziness or contractions as signs of excessive fatigue.
Monitor for symptoms of hypoglycemia or hypotension and avoid prolonged fasting.
Physiotherapeutic techniques must be done by qualified professionals with medical authorization, avoiding areas of uterine risk.
